intro: A p-value answers one question: if the null hypothesis were true, how surprising would a result like ours be? Drag the observed statistic and watch the shaded area, the p-value, grow and shrink. Then switch to Errors and power to see the two ways a test can be wrong and what makes it more likely to catch a real effect.
howItWorksTitle: How the pictures and numbers are made
howItWorks:
The curve is the null distribution: the sampling distribution of the statistic when $H_0$ is true. For a proportion it is the normal model with mean $p_0$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}$; for a mean it is the $t$ distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom. The shaded area is the p-value, computed exactly from that distribution, in the direction $H_a$ names.

  • One or two sided. A one-sided alternative shades one tail; a two-sided one shades both tails, beyond the observed value and its mirror image.
  • α. The dashed line is the cutoff: a statistic beyond it gives a p-value below α.
  • Errors and power. The second curve is the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ if the true proportion is the value you drag. The area of the null curve beyond the cutoff is α (Type I), the area of the true curve short of the cutoff is β (Type II), and the rest of the true curve is the power.
